dati_metodo: US VC-backed portfolio companies and VC funds, funding rounds 1980-1999 (exits tracked to Nov 2003); network centrality of syndication ties; fund-level exit-rate models and company-level probit models of survival to the next round (rounds 1-3).

righe.estrazione: The paper finds that better-networked VC firms have higher fund performance (share of investments exited via IPO or sale) and that their portfolio companies are significantly more likely to survive to a subsequent funding round and to exit. In each of the 15 probit models, better-networked lead investors go with higher survival probabilities. The authors note the link could partly reflect deal quality, and present evidence leaning toward a value-adding network channel.
righe.citazione: the portfolio companies of better-networked VCs are significantly more likely to survive to subsequent financing and eventual exit.
righe.frase_paper: Hochberg et al. (2007) find that US VC firms with better syndication networks have higher fund exit rates and that their portfolio companies are more likely to survive to later funding rounds and to exit (1980-1999 rounds).
righe.frase_slide: Better-networked VCs have higher exit rates; their companies more often reach later rounds (Hochberg et al., 2007)
righe.numero_chiave: One-standard-deviation rise in lead VC eigenvector centrality: round-1 survival 66.8% to 72.4%; round-2 survival 77.7% to 82.8%; round-3 survival 79.2% to 86.6%.
righe.limiti_vs_noi: Rounds 1980-1999, not 2012-2019; survival to next round is defined with write-off as zero; focus is on lead investor network position, not the gap between rounds.
righe.note: Tesi worded as 'perform better' and 'ventures survive': supported, as associations. The paper discusses selection of high-quality deals as an alternative reading.

righe.estrazione: The tesi is vague. The paper reports signs of lead-investor controls in its survival-to-next-round probits: lead fund size goes with higher survival, corporate-VC-led first rounds with lower survival, first-time lead funds with lower survival from round 3, and more experienced VCs with lower survival in rounds 2 and 3. It reports nothing on round-1 size or startup age as controls, and its outcome is survival to the next round or exit, not exit within five years.
righe.citazione: First-round investments led by corporate VCs (accounting for 5.7% of the sample rounds) are significantly less likely to survive.
righe.posizione: Section on company survival (Table V discussion)
righe.frase_paper: Hochberg et al. (2007) find that first rounds led by corporate VCs are significantly less likely to survive to the next round, in US VC-backed companies funded 1980-1999.
righe.frase_slide: Corporate-VC-led first rounds are less likely to survive to a next round (Hochberg et al., 2007)
righe.numero_chiave: Corporate-VC-led first rounds are 5.7% of the sample rounds.
righe.limiti_vs_noi: Outcome is survival to the next round (write-off = 0), not exit within five years; 1980-1999 sample; lead type, fund size and VC age are measured on the lead VC, no round-1 size or startup age control.
righe.note: Only the lead-type sign is comparable with our controls; no sign comparison is possible for round-1 size or age. Shared tesi with four other sources; judged only on this one.
